name: Long-Term Digital Preservation
title: Long-Term Digital Preservation
answer: Long-term digital preservation is the work of keeping digital objects usable, understandable, and trustworthy over decades, across changes in hardware, software, formats, and organizations. In research data and repositories, the objects include datasets, code, models, papers, metadata, and the documentation needed to interpret them. Preservation is not the same as backup, because it also manages format viability, context, and the chain of custody. The scope covers selection, ingest, storage, access, and periodic review for as long as the material has value.

crumbs.name: Knowledge Based Professions and their Future

sections.body: Long-term digital preservation is the work of keeping digital objects usable, understandable, and trustworthy over decades, across changes in hardware, software, formats, and organizations. In research data and repositories, the objects include datasets, code, models, papers, metadata, and the documentation needed to interpret them. Preservation is not the same as backup, because it also manages format viability, context, and the chain of custody. The scope covers selection, ingest, storage, access, and periodic review for as long as the material has value.
sections.heading: Scope

sections.body: Long-term preservation runs on layered storage, with disk for access, tape or cloud object storage for deep retention, and multiple copies in separate locations. Repository platforms such as DSpace, Fedora, and Dataverse manage deposits, versions, metadata, and access controls. Persistent identifiers, commonly DOIs, give each object a stable reference that survives moves between systems. Fixity services compute checksums and compare them over time to detect bit rot and media failure. The infrastructure also depends on documented formats, standard metadata schemas, and staff who can operate and migrate the stack.
sections.heading: What it runs on

sections.body: The work begins at ingest, when files are checked, described with metadata, and assigned a persistent identifier. Many repositories follow the OAIS reference model to separate submission, archival storage, data management, and access. Staff plan for format obsolescence by normalizing common formats to preservation-friendly ones such as PDF/A for text or plain text for tabular data. Over time they migrate content to new formats or emulate old environments when migration would lose meaning. Regular fixity audits and periodic policy reviews keep the collection trustworthy.
sections.heading: How the work is done

sections.body: Preservation raises rights questions because repositories often hold third-party data, licensed content, and personal information. Governance sets who may deposit, who may access, and under what terms, with licences and consent recorded alongside the object. Provenance metadata records origin, custody, and any changes, which supports authenticity and reproducibility. Risks include bit rot, format obsolescence, media failure, organizational change, and accidental deletion, and each needs a documented response. Clear agreements with depositors and users help prevent later disputes over access or reuse.
sections.heading: Rights, risk and provenance

sections.body: The field is moving toward more automated preservation, with machine learning used to extract metadata, detect format risks, and flag anomalies in large collections. Emulation and virtualization services are making it easier to re-run old software without keeping old hardware. Research repositories are also linking preservation more tightly with data management plans and reproducibility checks. The open questions are cost, energy use, and how to preserve AI models and their training data as those become common research outputs. Standards for machine-actionable provenance and long-term model archiving are still developing.
